Conclusions and Business Recommendations¶

Conclusions¶

In [81]:
# Key results at a glance - rendered from the live evaluation so the conclusions always match the run
display(Markdown(
    f"| Task Completion | Escalation Accuracy | Tool Call Accuracy | Coherence | Mean Latency |\n"
    f"|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n"
    f"| **{sum(task_flags) / n_cases:.0%}** | **{sum(esc_flags) / len(esc_flags):.0%}** | "
    f"**{sum(tool_flags) / n_cases:.0%}** | **{sum(coherence_scores) / n_cases:.2f} / 5** | "
    f"**{sum(latencies) / n_cases:.1f} s** |"
))
Task Completion Escalation Accuracy Tool Call Accuracy Coherence Mean Latency
100% 100% 100% 4.80 / 5 6.7 s
  • The full exception lifecycle can be automated end to end. From raw, noisy status logs, the multi-agent system deduplicates and consolidates events, separates routine noise from real exceptions, decides a policy-compliant resolution, escalates when the playbook requires it, and drafts a personalised customer message. Every step leaves an auditable trail: tool-call log, step-by-step rationale with playbook page citations, Critic verdicts, and LangSmith traces.
  • Hybrid design beats pure LLM or pure rules. Deterministic components handle what must never be wrong: deduplication, noise filtering, locker eligibility, prompt-injection blocking and the automatic escalation rules. LLMs handle what rules cannot: interpreting messy driver notes ("box crushed… visible dent"), grading damage severity for fragile items, and calibrating tone and content. In this run every required escalation came from an automatic trigger enforced in code, including the Section 1 second-attempt rule. That is why escalation accuracy does not depend on LLM judgment.
  • Noise costs nothing. Routine events are closed by the preprocessor with zero tool and zero LLM calls. At a ~10% exception rate, about 90% of the event stream never reaches a model, which keeps cost per event close to zero.
  • Independent validation adds a safety net. A separate, stronger model (the Critic) checks each decision and each customer message, and can send either back with specific feedback. In the revision-loop check, the Critic corrected a wrong decision (RESCHEDULE for a leaking perishable) to REPLACE in one loop. Both loops are bounded at two REVISE verdicts. A decision that keeps failing is escalated, and a message that keeps failing is held for human review instead of being sent, as happened for SHP-005 and SHP-007.
  • Tone and channel match the customer tier on every exception (8/8), following playbook Section 8. Messages explain what happened, what we are doing and what happens next, and acknowledge existing service credits without inventing amounts. PII stays limited to the Communication Agent.
  • Message validation is the least reliable component. It caught a real defect on SHP-007 (a promise to apply the $10 credit). It also flagged SHP-005 partly by misreading its own instruction, and it accepted SHP-003's SMS, which offers a re-attempt instead of asking the customer to verify the address.
  • Limitations of this POC:
    • The evaluation covers only 10 curated scenarios (8 exceptions), so a single miss changes a metric by 10–12.5 points.
    • LLM outputs can vary between runs, even at temperature 0.
    • The playbook has edge cases where the intended action had to be made explicit in the prompts, such as a 3rd attempt with a full locker and "didn't order it" refusals.
    • The Communication Agent and its Critic are not yet fully aligned on service-credit wording or on the "locker details will follow" case.

Business Recommendations¶

  • Pilot in shadow mode first. Run the system on live delivery feeds alongside human dispatchers for 4–6 weeks. Compare decisions, escalations and messages against staff outcomes on a much larger labelled set, and target ≥95% resolution accuracy with zero missed mandatory escalations. Then move to human-approved sending, and finally to autonomous handling of low-risk exceptions (1st/2nd failed attempts, weather delays on standard packages).
  • Tighten message validation before sending messages automatically.
    • Add deterministic checks for content each resolution requires. For example, an address-issue message must ask the customer to confirm the address within the 48/72-hour window, and SMS messages must stay within 320 characters.
    • Align the Communication Agent and Critic prompts on service-credit wording.
    • Until then, keep human approval for flagged messages, which the message_review_required flag already supports.
  • Keep mandatory policy in code and version it with the playbook. Each playbook update (thresholds such as "4 hours", "≥3 exceptions", locker rules) should update the rule engine and prompts together, with this evaluation suite as a regression gate before release. Encode the rules the playbook states outside its escalation matrix, as done here for the Section 1 second-attempt rule and for "3rd attempt + full locker → reroute via supervisor".
  • Invest in the data the decisions depend on. Add temperature-controlled lockers, search for lockers in adjacent zip codes (the playbook allows it; the current tool checks only the same zip), add a customer tone_preference field (referenced by the playbook but missing from the database), and capture structured damage and delay fields in the driver app, so less depends on parsing free text.
  • Use escalation data to fix root causes. Customers like CUST-011 (6 exceptions, 2nd and 3rd attempts) and CUST-001 (VIP, 5 exceptions) point to systemic problems: no buzzer, customer works late. Route these patterns to operations for proactive fixes (locker-first delivery preference, evening delivery windows), which reduces repeat truck rolls and churn among high-value customers.
  • Operationalise observability. Keep LangSmith tracing in production and track the five metrics on a dashboard, plus cost per exception, escalation rate and the share of messages held for review. Alert on coherence drops, rising revision loops or latency spikes, and review a weekly sample of Critic ESCALATE/REVISE decisions to tune prompts.
  • Scale deliberately. After the pilot, extend the exception taxonomy (lost, stolen, misrouted packages), add multi-language messaging and multi-region playbooks, and consider a cheaper model for the Communication Critic on low-severity cases to reduce cost per exception.
